findings.step: Read the male bar for 0-4 off the scale.  [box expects: 7.1]
findings.why: Nothing in this question (country-type-from-shape, MC) ever says the pyramid bars are percentages. The box has no unit and the final answer is a lettered MC choice with no unit either, so a student typing '7.1' has zero textual confirmation this is a percent-of-population reading rather than millions/thousands. Same problem repeats on the next three steps in this walk (0.8, 6.3, 13.8).
findings.fix: Show '%' to the right of the box on every bar-reading/adding step in this walk (7.1, 0.8, 6.3, 13.8), not just on problems whose final answer happens to be a percentage.

findings.step: How much longer is the 0-4 male bar than the 60-64 male bar?  [box expects: 6.3]
findings.why: 'Longer' frames this as a bar-length/physical-distance question, when the value being subtracted is actually a percentage-point difference. A student could reasonably think they need to measure the bars in cm.
findings.fix: Reword to "How much bigger is the 0-4 percentage than the 60-64 percentage?" and label the box '%'.

findings.step: Read the male bar for 0-4.  [box expects: 7.1] / Add them to get the whole 0-4 band. [box expects: 13.8]
findings.why: The question stem does say 'highest percentage of the population', so there's some context, but none of the four bar-reading/summing boxes in the walk itself repeat '%' — a student could still start entering raw-looking numbers without the percent frame in front of them at the moment of typing.
findings.fix: Add '%' to the box on every bar-read/sum step (7.1, 6.7, 13.8, 6.8).

findings.step: Now do the same for 30-34 to compare.  [box expects: 6.8]
findings.why: "Do the same" is a vague back-reference to a two-part process two steps back (read male bar, read female bar, add them) but only one number is asked for here. A student may read the male bar for 30-34 only and stop, not realising two bars need adding.
findings.fix: Spell it out: "Now read the male and female bars for 30-34 and add them together."

findings.step: Warm up on the row above it: read the male bar for 45-49. [box expects: 3.8] / Now read the male bar for 40-44. [box expects: 3.7]
findings.why: The question stem and main answer box already establish '%' for this problem, so context is strong, but the intermediate boxes still show no unit, breaking consistency with the final box.
findings.fix: Show '%' on the intermediate boxes too, purely for consistency.

findings.step: Add the two dependant groups together.  [box expects: 48]
findings.why: "The two dependant groups" is a back-reference to the 44% (given in the question) and the 4% (given two steps earlier) — neither number is restated here, so a student has to hold both in memory across steps.
findings.fix: "Add the under-15 group (44%) and the over-65 group (4%) together."

findings.step: Divide dependants by workers and multiply by 100. Give a whole number.  [box expects: 92]
findings.why: The previous three steps in this same walk were all percentages (44, 56, 48), so a student is primed to also append a '%' to this answer — but a dependency ratio is not a percentage, even though it's calculated the same way. There is no label to break that habit. "Give a whole number" is also vaguer than the "to the nearest whole number" phrasing used elsewhere in this lesson (e.g. gold[0], gold[3]), leaving rounding-vs-truncating unclear.
findings.fix: Label the box '(a ratio — no % sign)' and reword to "...multiply by 100, rounded to the nearest whole number."

findings.step: Check: take your ratio away from 100.  [box expects: 8]
findings.why: The step never explains what this arithmetic is actually checking, so a student can do the subtraction correctly without understanding why, or wonder if they've misread the task.
findings.fix: Add a one-clause reason, e.g. "As a rough sanity check, see how far below 100 your ratio sits."

findings.step: Counting the top bar as row 1 and working down, which row number is 65-69?  [box expects: 3]
findings.why: Every other pyramid problem in this lesson counts 'the bottom bar as row 1'. This problem silently flips the direction. A student who has just done several bottom-up problems is likely to apply the same habit here without noticing the switch.
findings.fix: Make the change explicit: "Unlike earlier questions, count from the TOP this time — the top bar is row 1."

findings.step: Add the three male bars for 65-69, 70-74 and 75+.  [box expects: 8.5]
findings.why: Main answer box already shows '%' so context is decent, but this and the next summing step (10.6) are unlabeled.
findings.fix: Add '%' to both intermediate sum boxes for consistency.

findings.step: Read the male bar for 0-4.  [box expects: 2] / Read the male bar for that widest row, 45-49. [box expects: 4.4]
findings.why: This question (Germany narrow base -> population decline, MC) never mentions percentages anywhere, and the MC final answer has no unit either. A student has no textual cue that 2 and 4.4 are percent-of-population readings.
findings.fix: Show '%' on both bar-reading boxes (and on the base-check sum, 3.8).

findings.step: How many times wider is the widest male bar than the 0-4 male bar?  [box expects: 2.2]
findings.why: This answer is a unitless multiplier (a ratio of two percentages), but coming right after two unlabeled percentage-reading steps, a student could easily assume it's also a percentage and second-guess a correct '2.2'.
findings.fix: Label the box '(a multiplier, e.g. 2.2 — not a %)'.

findings.step: How many rows are there from 15-19 up to 60-64 inclusive?  [box expects: 10]
findings.why: The walk only ever establishes the row number for 15-19 (row 4). It never asks for, or states, the row number for 60-64 (row 13). To answer '10' the student must silently work out the second endpoint's row themselves and then do inclusive counting — a skill never demonstrated earlier in the walk.
findings.fix: Insert a step first: "Which row number is 60-64?" so both endpoints are on the table before asking for the inclusive count.

findings.step: Add the male bars for those ten rows.  [box expects: 30.0] / Now add the female bars for the same ten rows. [box expects: 26.2]
findings.why: Main box shows '%', giving decent context, but these two summing boxes are unlabeled.
findings.fix: Add '%' to both boxes.

findings.step: Now divide dependants by workers and multiply by 100, to the nearest whole number.  [box expects: 85]
findings.why: Same ratio-vs-percentage confusion as bronze[6]: the two steps immediately before this were percentages (46%, 54%), so the habit of expecting a % carries over even though the correct main-box unit here is '(none)'.
findings.fix: Label the box '(a ratio, not a %)'.

findings.step: The narrowing base holds children born in the last five years, so from which year onwards?  [box expects: 2020]
findings.why: Getting 2020 requires remembering '2025' as the survey year, which was stated three steps earlier in the walk's intro and never restated here.
findings.fix: "Using 2025 as the survey year again, the narrowing base holds children born in the last five years — so from which year onwards?"

findings.step: Divide dependants by workers and multiply by 100, to the nearest whole number.  [box expects: 89]
findings.why: Same recurring ratio-vs-% issue: preceding steps (47%, 53%) are percentages, this one is not, and the box carries no label to signal the change.
findings.fix: Label the box '(a ratio, not a %)'.

findings.step: Check: take your new ratio away from 100.  [box expects: 11]
findings.why: As with bronze[6], the purpose of subtracting from 100 is never explained, so the check step teaches nothing to a student who does it correctly.
findings.fix: Add a short reason for the check, or drop it if it isn't pedagogically necessary.

findings.step: And someone aged 65 today?  [box expects: 85]
findings.why: Sentence fragment leaning entirely on the previous full sentence's template ('...will be how old in 20 years?'). Usually inferable, but strictly incomplete.
findings.fix: "And how old will someone aged 65 today be in 20 years?"

findings.step: And someone aged 35?  [box expects: 1990]
findings.why: Same ellipsis pattern as bronze[5] — relies on the prior sentence's structure ('...was born in which year?').
findings.fix: "And someone aged 35 — which year were they born?"

findings.step: And someone aged 30?  [box expects: 1995]
findings.why: Same recurring ellipsis pattern.
findings.fix: "And someone aged 30 — which year were they born?"

findings.step: And someone aged 80?  [box expects: 1935]
findings.why: Same recurring ellipsis pattern.
findings.fix: "And someone aged 80 — which year were they born?"

findings.step: Parkland and industrial each appear how many times?  [box expects: 1]
findings.why: The plural framing ('Parkland and industrial each appear...') reads like it wants two separate counts, when actually only one shared number is expected because both happen to tie.
findings.fix: "Parkland and industrial both appear the same number of times — how many is that?"

findings.step: Q1 is the middle of the lower four, so average the 2nd and 3rd sorted values. What is Q1 in m/s?  [box expects: 0.85]
findings.why: The eight velocities are given unsorted in the question (0.8, 1.2, 0.9, 1.5, 1.1, 1.3, 0.7, 1.0). The walk never displays the sorted order, so the student must correctly sort all eight in their head before they can even find 'the 2nd and 3rd sorted values'. A sorting slip breaks everything downstream.
findings.fix: Show the sorted list explicitly: "Sorted: 0.7, 0.8, 0.9, 1.0, 1.1, 1.2, 1.3, 1.5."

findings.step: Which beach has the smaller range? Type 1 for Beach A or 2 for Beach B.  [box expects: 2]
findings.why: Every other box in this lesson expects a real measurement value. This step suddenly switches to an arbitrary numeric code (1/2) for a letter choice, which is a different convention a student hasn't been primed for — they may type 'A'/'B' or the range value instead of '2'.
findings.fix: Accept the letter directly: "Type A or B."

findings.step: Q1 is the middle of the lower six, so average the 3rd and 4th sorted values. What is Q1, in metres?  [box expects: 2.85]
findings.why: Twelve unsorted river-width values (2.1, 3.4, 2.8, 5.2, 3.1, 2.5, 4.8, 3.6, 2.9, 3.3, 4.1, 3.0) must be mentally sorted with zero scaffolding shown — harder than the 8-value silver version of the same problem type, and a single misordering invalidates Q1, Q3 and the IQR.
findings.fix: Display the sorted list before asking for Q1: "Sorted: 2.1, 2.5, 2.8, 2.9, 3.0, 3.1, 3.3, 3.4, 3.6, 4.1, 4.8, 5.2."

findings.step: Sorted, the middle pair sit in positions 5 and 6. Average them to get the median, in ppm.  [box expects: 402.5]
findings.why: Ten unsorted CO2 readings (including the extreme outlier 1200) must be sorted mentally before the student can find positions 5 and 6 — the sorted list is never shown, unlike some other problems in this lesson (e.g. silver[6]) that do show it.

findings.step: Subtract Q1 from Q3 to get the IQR, then check it comes out below the full range of 23.  [box expects: 13]
findings.why: The sentence bundles two instructions (compute the IQR; verify a check against the range) but there is only one answer box. A student may be unsure whether the check itself needs a typed response, or may try to type something related to '23'.
findings.fix: End the question at "Subtract Q1 from Q3 to get the IQR." and present the range comparison as separate feedback text after the answer is submitted, not as part of the instruction.

findings.step: Subtract Q1 from Q3 to get the IQR, then check it comes out below the full range of 14.  [box expects: 8]
findings.why: Same compound-instruction pattern as bronze[7] — one box, two asks.
findings.fix: Split the check out of the question text, as above.

findings.step: Subtract Q1 from Q3 to get the IQR, then check it comes out below the full range of 3.2.  [box expects: 1.7]
findings.why: Same compound-instruction pattern recurring a third time in this lesson.
findings.fix: Split the check out of the question text, as above.

findings.step: Add the two middle values of that upper half, the 3rd and 4th of the six.  [box expects: 31]
findings.why: The question explicitly instructs 'First put in order, then find Q3', flagging that the raw data (given in calendar order, with two repeated values — 6 and 8 each appear twice) needs reordering. But the walk only ever confirms the smallest value (5); the full sorted list is never shown. The student must correctly reorder all twelve values, including the duplicates, entirely unaided before they can isolate 'the 3rd and 4th of the six' in the upper half.
findings.fix: Show the full sorted list: "Sorted: 5, 6, 6, 8, 8, 10, 12, 13, 15, 16, 17, 18."

findings.step: Find the row labelled Urban. Reading down to the scale, what value does the left edge of its shaded box sit on?  [box expects: 18]
findings.why: The value read is a temperature (matching the main box's °C), but this box-plot-reading step doesn't restate the unit the way the equivalent gold[0] problem does ('in metres').
findings.fix: Add '°C' to this step and the next one (right edge, 31), matching the phrasing used in gold[0].

findings.step: QUESTION: ...An outlier is defined as more than 1.5 × IQR above Q3. Is 15.8 an outlier? Enter Q3 + 1.5 × IQR (the outlier boundary).
findings.why: The question leads with a yes/no-shaped question ('Is 15.8 an outlier?') but the actual required answer is a specific number — the boundary value, 24.25 — not a yes/no judgement and not 15.8 itself. A student reading top-to-bottom is very likely to try answering the rhetorical question literally.
findings.fix: Remove or clearly subordinate the framing question, e.g.: "An outlier is more than 1.5×IQR above Q3. Calculate the outlier boundary (Q3 + 1.5×IQR) so you can check whether 15.8 counts as one."

findings.step: Add that to Q3 to get the boundary, then compare it with the largest value of 15.8.  [box expects: 24.25]
findings.why: Same compound-instruction issue as the bronze[7]/silver[6]/gold[2] pattern, and it compounds the question-level ambiguity above (finding for the gold[3] question stem) about whether a comparison verdict is also expected.
findings.fix: End the instruction at "...to get the boundary." and drop the comparison clause from the graded step.

findings.step: The lower half is the five values below the median. Give its middle value. This is Q1.  [box expects: -8]
findings.why: This is the first negative answer in either lesson pack, introduced with no warning that a negative value is expected. The eleven mixed-sign migration values are also never shown in sorted order, so the student must both sort numbers with mixed signs and correctly type a negative result, unaided, for the first time here.
findings.fix: Show the sorted list and flag the sign explicitly: "Sorted: -45, -20, -8, 5, 12, 25, 38, 52, 71, 95, 120 — note some values are negative."
